claim: Memory consolidation during sleep depends on the interregional coupling of slow waves, spindles, and sharp wave-ripples (SWRs), across the cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus.
source: Memory consolidation during sleep depends on the interregional coupling of slow waves, spindles, and sharp wave-ripples (SWRs), across the cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about sleep-dependent memory consolidation mechanisms.

claim: The reuniens nucleus of the thalamus links the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the hippocampus.
source: The reuniens nucleus of the thalamus, linking the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the hippocampus, may facilitate interregional coupling during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the reuniens evoked both antidromic and orthodromic intracellular mPFC responses.
source: Electrical stimulation of the reuniens evoked both antidromic and orthodromic intracellular mPFC responses, consistent with bidirectional functional connectivity between mPFC, reuniens and hippocampus in anesthetized state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings in anesthetized cats.

claim: During NREM sleep hippocampo-reuniens-mPFC form a functional loop.
source: The major finding obtained from behaving animals is that at least during NREM sleep hippocampo-reuniens-mPFC form a functional loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behaving animals during NREM sleep.

claim: SWRs facilitate the triggering of thalamic spindles, which later reach neocortex.
source: SWRs facilitate the triggering of thalamic spindles, which later reach neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of temporal relationships between SWRs and spindles.

claim: Transition to mPFC UP states increase the probability of hippocampal SWRs and later modulate spindle amplitude.
source: In return, transition to mPFC UP states increase the probability of hippocampal SWRs and later modulate spindle amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing phase-locking relationships between mPFC slow waves and SWRs.

claim: During REM sleep hippocampal theta activity provides periodic locking of reuniens neuronal firing.
source: During REM sleep hippocampal theta activity provides periodic locking of reuniens neuronal firing and strong crosscorrelation at LFP level, but the values of reuniens-mPFC crosscorrelation was relatively low and theta power at mPFC was low.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from REM sleep recordings showing phase-locking of reuniens neurons to hippocampal theta.

claim: The strength of bidirectional hippocampo-thalamic connections determines the coupling of oscillations.
source: The neural mass model of this network demonstrates that the strength of bidirectional hippocampo-thalamic connections determines the coupling of oscillations, suggesting a mechanistic link between synaptic weights and the propensity for interregional synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: The efficacy of hippocampo-thalamo-cortical connectivity is modulated by behavioral state.
source: Our results demonstrate the presence of functional connectivity in hippocampo-thalamo-cortical network, but the efficacy of this connectivity is modulated by behavioral state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different patterns of connectivity during wake, NREM, and REM sleep.

claim: Slow waves (SWs) occur at 0.1–4 Hz.
source: During sleep, hippocampal and cortical activity is continually synchronized by cardinal sleep oscillations such as slow waves (SWs, 0.1–4 Hz), thalamocortical spindles (10–15 Hz), and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs, 100–300 Hz; Isomura et al., 2006; Siapas and Wilson, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Thalamocortical spindles occur at 10–15 Hz.
source: During sleep, hippocampal and cortical activity is continually synchronized by cardinal sleep oscillations such as slow waves (SWs, 0.1–4 Hz), thalamocortical spindles (10–15 Hz), and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs, 100–300 Hz; Isomura et al., 2006; Siapas and Wilson, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) occur at 100–300 Hz.
source: During sleep, hippocampal and cortical activity is continually synchronized by cardinal sleep oscillations such as slow waves (SWs, 0.1–4 Hz), thalamocortical spindles (10–15 Hz), and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs, 100–300 Hz; Isomura et al., 2006; Siapas and Wilson, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Sleep rhythms have well-known roles in neuronal plasticity.
source: These rhythms have well-known roles in neuronal plasticity (Chauvette et al., 2012; Diekelmann and Born, 2010) and in the consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories (Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sleep rhythms have well-known roles in the consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories.
source: These rhythms have well-known roles in neuronal plasticity (Chauvette et al., 2012; Diekelmann and Born, 2010) and in the consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories (Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hierarchical coupling of slow waves, spindles and SWRs is thought to play a key role in memory consolidation.
source: In particular, the hierarchical coupling of slow waves, spindles and SWRs is thought to play a key role in memory consolidation (Diekelmann and Born, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The temporal coupling of hippocampal and mPFC sleep oscillations results in a selective increase in the recall of hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the temporal coupling of hippocampal and mPFC sleep oscillations results in a selective increase in the recall of hippocampus-dependent memory (Latchoumane et al., 2017; Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus extends projections to several prefrontal areas.
source: Although the hippocampus extends projections to several prefrontal areas (Cavada et al., 1983; Goldman-Rakic et al., 1984; Irle and Markowitsch, 1982; Jay and Witter, 1991; Swanson, 1981), few regions of the prefrontal cortex reciprocate (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Few regions of the prefrontal cortex reciprocate projections to the hippocampus.
source: Although the hippocampus extends projections to several prefrontal areas (Cavada et al., 1983; Goldman-Rakic et al., 1984; Irle and Markowitsch, 1982; Jay and Witter, 1991; Swanson, 1981), few regions of the prefrontal cortex reciprocate (Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: No direct projections from medial regions of the prefrontal cortex to the hippocampus have been identified.
source: With respect to medial regions of the prefrontal cortex, no direct projections to the hippocampus have been identified (Beckstead, 1979; Goldman-Rakic et al., 1984; Reep et al., 1987; Room et al., 1985; Takagishi and Chiba, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The nucleus reuniens of the thalamus (reuniens) is bidirectionally connected to the hippocampus and the mPFC.
source: The nucleus reuniens of the thalamus (reuniens) is bidirectionally connected to the hippocampus and the mPFC (Herkenham, 1978; Vertes et al., 2007), making it an ideal hub for coupling hippocampo-cortical interactions during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Reuniens is part of the ventral group of midline thalamic nuclei with widespread connections to cortical, thalamic, hypothalamic and brainstem structures.
source: Reuniens is part of the ventral group of midline thalamic nuclei with widespread connections to cortical, thalamic, hypothalamic and brainstem structures (Herkenham, 1978; McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Ohtake and Yamada, 1989; Robertson and Kaitz, 1981; Vertes et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Reuniens plays a major role for memory function.
source: Consistent with its anatomical connections to the hippocampus and the mPFC, reuniens plays a major role for memory function (Ramanathan et al., 2018; Xu and Südhof, 2013) and a growing body of evidence points its critical role in processing hippocampus-dependent memory (Ramanathan and Maren, 2019; Ramanathan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A growing body of evidence points to reuniens' critical role in processing hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: Consistent with its anatomical connections to the hippocampus and the mPFC, reuniens plays a major role for memory function (Ramanathan et al., 2018; Xu and Südhof, 2013) and a growing body of evidence points its critical role in processing hippocampus-dependent memory (Ramanathan and Maren, 2019; Ramanathan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Little is known about the nature of reuniens-prefrontal interactions and their interplay with hippocampal events during sleep.
source: Although evidence for the functional significance of reuniens in cognitive operations is strong, little is known about the nature of reuniens-prefrontal interactions and their interplay with hippocampal events during sleep (Di Prisco and Vertes, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a knowledge gap.

claim: Stimulation of the hippocampus and reuniens elicited synaptic responses in 55% and 51% of recorded mPFC neurons, respectively.
source: Stimulation of the hippocampus and reuniens elicited synaptic responses in 55% and 51% of recorded mPFC neurons, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Hippocampal stimulation generated variable responses in the same neurons, consisting of complex sequences of either two excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) followed by long-lasting hyperpolarization, a depolarization-hyperpolarization sequence, or no response.
source: Hippocampal stimulation generated variable responses in the same neurons, consisting of complex sequences of either two excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) followed by long-lasting hyperpolarization (Figure 1E, top, left), a depolarization-hyperpolarization sequence (Figure 1E, middle, left), or no response (Figure 1E, bottom, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The polarity of early depolarizing responses elicited by hippocampal stimulation was dependent on membrane potential, reversing with progressive depolarization of the membrane at around –70 mV.
source: The polarity of early depolarizing responses elicited by hippocampal stimulation was dependent on membrane potential, reversing with progressive depolarization of the membrane at around –70 mV (Figure 1E, right), suggesting that the initial depolarization was an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The initial depolarization elicited by hippocampal stimulation was an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP).
source: The polarity of early depolarizing responses elicited by hippocampal stimulation was dependent on membrane potential, reversing with progressive depolarization of the membrane at around –70 mV (Figure 1E, right), suggesting that the initial depolarization was an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the voltage-dependent reversal of the response.

claim: Reuniens stimulation elicited consistent EPSPs followed by long-lasting hyperpolarization at earlier latencies than hippocampal stimulation (6.05±3.6ms for reuniens and 9.95±4.6ms for hippocampal stimulation, respectively, t-test, p<0.01).
source: Reuniens stimulation elicited consistent EPSPs followed by long-lasting hyperpolarization (Figure 1C, bottom) at earlier latencies than hippocampal stimulation (6.05±3.6ms for reuniens and 9.95±4.6ms and hippocampal stimulation, respectively, t-test, p<0.01, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1G.

claim: EPSPs elicited by reuniens stimulation had faster rising slopes compared to hippocampal stimulation (0.56±0.27 V/s for reuniens and 1.9±0.9 V/s for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01).
source: EPSPs elicited by reuniens stimulation had faster rising slopes compared to hippocampal stimulation (0.56±0.27 V/s for reuniens and 1.9±0.9 V/s for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01) but were of lower amplitude (3.1±2.0 mV for reuniens and 8.4±4.1 mV for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: EPSPs elicited by reuniens stimulation were of lower amplitude than those elicited by hippocampal stimulation (3.1±2.0 mV for reuniens and 8.4±4.1 mV for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01).
source: EPSPs elicited by reuniens stimulation had faster rising slopes compared to hippocampal stimulation (0.56±0.27 V/s for reuniens and 1.9±0.9 V/s for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01) but were of lower amplitude (3.1±2.0 mV for reuniens and 8.4±4.1 mV for hippocampal stimulation, t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: There was no significant difference in the duration of the late, hyperpolarizing component in response to reuniens and hippocampal stimulations.
source: We observed no significant difference in the duration of the late, hyperpolarizing component in response to reuniens and hippocampal stimulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Reuniens stimulation elicited action potentials that were either orthodromic (85%), antidromic (10%) or both (5%).
source: Reuniens stimulation elicited action potentials that were either orthodromic (85%), antidromic (10%) or both (5%), evidenced by jitter in the latency of orthodromic action potentials and consistent latency of antidromic action potentials (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Antidromic responses to reuniens stimulation were recorded in cells located 6050–6600 μm ventral to the dorsal aspect of the cortical surface.
source: Antidromic responses to reuniens stimulation, confirmed by collision tests, were recorded in cells located 6050–6600 μm ventral to the dorsal aspect of the cortical surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: The mean latency of antidromic spikes was 2.9±0.25ms (mean ± SD).
source: The mean latency of antidromic spikes was 2.9±0.25ms (mean ± SD).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Reuniens stimulation evoked field postsynaptic potential in a wider prefrontal territory compared to hippocampal stimulation which was restricted to the ventroposterior part of the mPFC.
source: Reuniens stimulation evoked field postsynaptic potential in a wider prefrontal territory compared to hippocampal stimulation which was restricted to the ventroposterior part of the mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from field potential recordings.

claim: Areas in the prefrontal cortex that responded to hippocampal stimulation overlapped with areas exhibiting antidromic responses to reuniens stimulation.
source: Areas in the prefrontal cortex that responded to hippocampal stimulation overlapped with areas exhibiting antidromic responses to reuniens stimulation (Figure 1I, shadowed area) which corresponds to area 32 of the prelimbic cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The overlapping area of hippocampal and reuniens responses corresponds to area 32 of the prelimbic cortex.
source: Areas in the prefrontal cortex that responded to hippocampal stimulation overlapped with areas exhibiting antidromic responses to reuniens stimulation (Figure 1I, shadowed area) which corresponds to area 32 of the prelimbic cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: Reuniens spindles had significantly earlier onset relative to the onset of mPFC spindles (median = –0.083 s, n=49 sessions).
source: We observed co-occurring reuniens and mPFC spindles (Figure 2F), characterized by significantly earlier onset of reuniens spindles relative to the onset of mPFC spindles (median = –0.083 s, n=49 sessions, Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Reuniens single-unit activity exhibited significant phase-locking to mPFC spindle cycles (n=24/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –80.87±41.64°, p=2.942 x 10–7, Rayleigh test).
source: NREM sleep analysis of reuniens single-unit activity relative to the phase of mPFC and reuniens spindle cycles revealed significant phase-locking of reuniens single-units to mPFC spindle cycles (n=24/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –80.87±41.64°, p=2.942 x 10–7, Rayleigh test, Figure 2H) and reuniens spindle cycles (n=29/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –118.25±47.72°, p=1.047 x 10–6, Rayleigh test Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Reuniens single-unit activity exhibited significant phase-locking to reuniens spindle cycles (n=29/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –118.25±47.72°, p=1.047 x 10–6, Rayleigh test).
source: NREM sleep analysis of reuniens single-unit activity relative to the phase of mPFC and reuniens spindle cycles revealed significant phase-locking of reuniens single-units to mPFC spindle cycles (n=24/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –80.87±41.64°, p=2.942 x 10–7, Rayleigh test, Figure 2H) and reuniens spindle cycles (n=29/49 single-units, mean ± SD = –118.25±47.72°, p=1.047 x 10–6, Rayleigh test Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The mean phase preference of reuniens single-units was advanced for reuniens spindle cycles relative to mPFC spindle cycles.
source: The mean phase preference of reuniens single-units was advanced for reuniens spindle cycles relative to mPFC spindle cycles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing phase preferences.

claim: For pairs of co-occurring reuniens and mPFC spindles, spindle amplitudes were significantly correlated (r=0.54 using mPFC spindle as reference, p=3.22 × 10–27, and r=0.47, p=8.61 × 10–25 when using Reuniens spindle as reference).
source: For pairs of co-occurring reuniens and mPFC spindles, spindle amplitudes were significantly correlated (r=0.54 using mPFC spindle as reference, p=3.22 × 10–27, Figure 2J, and r=0.47, p=8.61 × 10–25 when using Reuniens spindle as reference, Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claim: Increased hippocampal ripple power and increased reuniens spindle power preceded the onset of spindles in the mPFC.
source: Lastly, we investigated during NREM sleep the change in hippocampal and reuniens signal power during mPFC spindles relative to baseline, which demonstrated increased hippocampal ripple power and increased reuniens spindle power preceding the onset of spindles in the mPFC (Figure 2L, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: SWR incidence was significantly higher in the 250ms window prior to the onset of mPFC spindles compared to shuffled data (t-test, p<0.05).
source: Compared to shuffled data, SWR rate was significantly higher in the 250ms window prior to the onset of mPFC spindles (t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing real and shuffled data.

claim: Reuniens multi-unit activity increased prior to the onset of mPFC spindles.
source: Reuniens multi-unit activity increased prior to the onset of mPFC spindles (Figure 2L, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The strength of slow wave-spindle coupling was higher for mPFC slow wave-reuniens spindle coupling compared to mPFC slow wave-mPFC spindle coupling (median ± MAD, SI strength = 0.18 ± 0.09 and 0.24±0.11 for mPFC and reuniens spindles, respectively, p=2.126 x 10–17, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: The strength of slow wave-spindle coupling, estimated by the absolute value of the synchronization index (SI) was higher for mPFC slow wave-reuniens spindle coupling compared to mPFC slow wave-mPFC spindle coupling (median ± mean absolute deviation [MAD], SI strength = 0.18 ± 0.09 and 0.24±0.11 for mPFC and reuniens spindles, respectively, p=2.126 x 10–17, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The amplitude of reuniens spindles increased at earlier phases of the mPFC slow wave compared to the amplitude of mPFC spindles.
source: The amplitude of reuniens spindles increased at earlier phases of the mPFC slow wave compared to the amplitude of mPFC spindles, which increased at later phases of the mPFC slow wave (Figure 3B, C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B, C, and F.

claim: mPFC can trigger reuniens spindles, but spindles recorded in mPFC are not necessarily imposed by reuniens spindles.
source: This finding suggests that mPFC can trigger reuniens spindles, but spindles recorded in mPFC are not necessarily imposed by reuniens spindles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phase-amplitude coupling data.

claim: Reuniens slow waves lagged mPFC slow waves (median ±MAD = 0.126±0.043 s, p=3.66 x 10–15, n=82, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: Single session data in Figure 3H demonstrates the delay between reuniens and mPFC slow waves, showing significant lag in the time of reuniens slow waves relative to mPFC slow waves (median ±MAD = 0.126±0.043 s, p=3.66 x 10–15, n=82, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The distribution of slow wave phases at the time of SWRs was non-uniform, indicating significant phase-locking of SWRs to mPFC slow waves at a mean phase of 162.7±29.37° (p=5.02 x 10–6, Rayleigh test).
source: The distribution of slow wave phases at the time of SWRs was non-uniform, indicating significant phase-locking of SWRs to mPFC slow waves at a mean phase of 162.7±29.37° (p=5.02 x 10–6, Rayleigh test, Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: There was no significant phase-locking of SWRs to spindle cycles in the majority of recording sessions (n=3/51 with significant phase for mPFC spindle-SWR and n=10/51 sessions with significant phase for reuniens spindle-SWR coupling).
source: We found no significant phase-locking of SWRs to spindle cycles in the majority of recording sessions (n=3/51 with significant phase for mPFC spindle-SWR and n=10/51 sessions with significant phase for reuniens spindle-SWR coupling, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: Reuniens single-unit activity exhibited significant phase-locking to the theta rhythm during REM (n=21/36 single-units, mean ± SD = –124.5±59.8°, p=0.011, Rayleigh test).
source: Analysis of reuniens firing around the peak of hippocampal theta cycles, shows significant phase-locking of reuniens single-unit activity to the theta rhythm during REM (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-F.

claim: mPFC signals lagged hippocampal signals by a longer delay than reuniens signals lagged hippocampus (mean lag ± SD = 87.8±55.5ms and 109.1±41.52 for reuniens and mPFC, respectively, n=20 sessions, p=0.002, t-test).
source: mPFC signals lagged hippocampal signals by a longer delay than reuniens signals lagged hippocampus (mean lag ± SD = 87.8±55.5ms and 109.1±41.52 for reuniens and mPFC, respectively, n=20 sessions, p=0.002, t-test, Figure 4J, top) and peak cross-correlation coefficients were significantly higher for reuniens-hippocampus recording pairs than for reuniens-mPFC (mean peak value ± SD = 0.44±0.13 and 0.22±0.07 for reuniens and mPFC respectively = 20 sessions, t-test, p<10–20, Figure 4J, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Peak cross-correlation coefficients were significantly higher for reuniens-hippocampus recording pairs than for reuniens-mPFC (mean peak value ± SD = 0.44±0.13 and 0.22±0.07 for reuniens and mPFC respectively = 20 sessions, t-test, p<10–20).
source: mPFC signals lagged hippocampal signals by a longer delay than reuniens signals lagged hippocampus (mean lag ± SD = 87.8±55.5ms and 109.1±41.52 for reuniens and mPFC, respectively, n=20 sessions, p=0.002, t-test, Figure 4J, top) and peak cross-correlation coefficients were significantly higher for reuniens-hippocampus recording pairs than for reuniens-mPFC (mean peak value ± SD = 0.44±0.13 and 0.22±0.07 for reuniens and mPFC respectively = 20 sessions, t-test, p<10–20, Figure 4J, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: In 20.4% of reuniens single-units (10/49), firing rate increased significantly following the onset of SWRs in the hippocampus, compared to shuffled events in the same period.
source: In 20.4% of reuniens single-units (10/49), firing rate increased significantly following the onset of SWRs in the hippocampus, compared to shuffled events in the same period (Figure 4L, 150 ms post-SWR onset).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Firing rates decreased significantly in 32.6% (16/49) of single-units following SWR onset.
source: Firing rates decreased significantly in 32.6% (16/49) of single-units following SWR onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peri-event analysis.

claim: The average thalamic LFP around the onset of the SWR was characterized by a negative, 250 μV deflection coincident with increased reuniens firing.
source: The average thalamic LFP around the onset of the SWR was characterized by a negative, 250 μV deflection coincident with increased reuniens firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings.

claim: Reuniens slow waves occur significantly later than cortical slow waves (median ± MAD = 0.113±0.019 s, p<10−20, Wilcoxon signed rank test) in the computational model.
source: We found that reuniens slow waves occur significantly later than cortical slow waves (median ± MAD = 0.113±0.019 s, p<10−20, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Thalamic spindles occur significantly earlier than cortical spindles (median ± MAD = –0.102±0.387 s, p=1.30 × 10−7, Wilcoxon signed rank test) in the computational model.
source: In contrast, thalamic spindles occur significantly earlier than cortical spindles (median ± MAD = –0.102±0.387 s, p=1.30 × 10−7, Wilcoxon signed rank test, Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the computational model, the slow wave-spindle coupling strength is higher for reuniens than cortical spindles (median ±MAD SI strength = 0.58 ± 0.11 and 0.66±0.15 for mPFC and reuniens, respectively, p=8.45 × 10−9, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: The slow wave-spindle coupling strength is also higher for reuniens than cortical spindles median ±MAD SI strength = 0.58 ± 0.11 and 0.66±0.15 for mPFC and reuniens, respectively, p=8.45 × 10−9, Wilcoxon signed rank test, (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In the computational model, SWRs are phase-locked to slow waves, occurring mainly before slow wave peaks (mean ± SD = –24.97±62.01°, p<10−20, Rayleigh test).
source: Phase locking analysis revealed that, consistent with the experimental data, SWRs are phase-locked to slow waves, occurring mainly before slow wave peaks (active phase, mean ± SD = –24.97±62.01°, p<10−20, Rayleigh test, (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The correlation between reuniens and CA1 membrane potentials during SWRs increased by increasing the strength of CA1 to reuniens projections in the computational model.
source: The correlation between reuniens and CA1 membrane potentials during SWRs increased by increasing the strength of CA1 to reuniens projections (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The SWR activity before spindle onset is an increasing function of bidirectional projections between CA1 and reuniens in the computational model.
source: In addition, the SWR activity before spindle onset is an increasing function of bidirectional projections between CA1 and reuniens (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The peak-to-trough magnitude of CA1 deflections around the cortical slow wave increases by increasing the reuniens-CA1 bidirectional projections in the computational model.
source: Next, we studied the effect of the strength of reuniens-CA1 bidirectional projections on CA1 activity during cortical slow waves. The peak-to-trough magnitude of CA1 deflections around the cortical slow wave also increases by increasing the reuniens-CA1 bidirectional projections (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The slow wave mean phase at the time of SWR occurrence decreased by increasing the strength of the bidirectional projections between reuniens and CA1 in the computational model.
source: The slow wave mean phase at the time of SWR occurrence decreased by increasing the strength of the bidirectional projections between reuniens and CA1 so that SWRs mostly occur before and after slow wave peak for strong and weak projections, respectively (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For strong reuniens-CA1 projection, the depolarizing input from reuniens during down-to-up transition is large enough to induce the SWRs in CA1 before the slow wave peak.
source: These results suggest that for strong reuniens-CA1 projection, the depolarizing input from reuniens during down-to-up transition is large enough to induce the SWRs in CA1 before the slow wave peak.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the computational modeling results.

claim: Reuniens activity during natural sleep was strongly modulated by hippocampal oscillations.
source: We found that reuniens activity during natural sleep was strongly modulated by hippocampal oscillations, and that reuniens-mPFC spindles were preceded by increased probability of hippocampal SWRs and ripple power.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chronic recordings.

claim: Reuniens-mPFC spindles were preceded by increased probability of hippocampal SWRs and ripple power.
source: We found that reuniens activity during natural sleep was strongly modulated by hippocampal oscillations, and that reuniens-mPFC spindles were preceded by increased probability of hippocampal SWRs and ripple power.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chronic recordings.

claim: Electrical stimulation of reuniens generated orthodromic and antidromic spiking in mPFC neurons, indicating bidirectional thalamocortical circuitry between the mPFC and reuniens.
source: Electrical stimulation of reuniens generated orthodromic and antidromic spiking in mPFC neurons, indicating bidirectional thalamocortical circuitry between the mPFC and reuniens.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Slow waves in reuniens lagged prefrontal slow waves but spindles in reuniens led prefrontal spindles.
source: Slow waves in reuniens lagged prefrontal slow waves but spindles in reuniens led prefrontal spindles, suggesting a bidirectional, oscillation-dependent dialogue between reuniens and the mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chronic recordings.

claim: Spindle amplitude and SWR occurrence was modulated by the phase of the prefrontal slow oscillation.
source: Spindle amplitude and SWR occurrence was modulated by the phase of the prefrontal slow oscillation, consistent with the idea that prefrontal slow waves control the timing of thalamic and hippocampal events.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing phase-amplitude coupling.

claim: Prefrontal slow waves control the timing of thalamic and hippocampal events.

claim: Reuniens is a core mediator in hippocampo-cortical dialogue.
source: Overall, the study provides physiological confirmation to the hypothesis that reuniens is a core mediator in hippocampo-cortical dialogue.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Response latency in the hippocampo-prefrontal pathway exhibits substantial variability.
source: Previous research has shown that response latency in the hippocampo-prefrontal pathway exhibits substantial variability (Dégenètais et al., 2003), indicating the involvement of both monosynaptic and polysynaptic mechanisms in prefrontal response to hippocampal input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Both monosynaptic and polysynaptic mechanisms are involved in prefrontal response to hippocampal input.
source: Previous research has shown that response latency in the hippocampo-prefrontal pathway exhibits substantial variability (Dégenètais et al., 2003), indicating the involvement of both monosynaptic and polysynaptic mechanisms in prefrontal response to hippocampal input.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the variability in response latency.

claim: Inconsistent mPFC responses to hippocampal stimulation were possibly due to inhibitory mechanisms such as shunting/feedforward inhibition or cholinergic, monoaminergic, or thalamic gating mechanisms.
source: This was possibly due to inhibitory mechanisms such as shunting/feedforward inhibition or cholinergic, monoaminergic, or thalamic gating mechanisms (Floresco and Grace, 2003; Gigg et al., 1994; Gioanni et al., 1999; Mansvelder et al., 2009; Robbins, 2005; Williams and Goldman-Rakic, 1995).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous research on gating mechanisms.

claim: Half of recorded prefrontal cells responded to reuniens stimulation.
source: In our study, half of recorded prefrontal cells responded to reuniens stimulation, with a mean response latency of 6ms and with antidromic spikes with a latency of approximately 3ms, pointing to bidirectional functional connectivity between the two structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intracellular recordings.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the reuniens/rhomboid nucleus in rats elicits prominent evoked potentials in prefrontal cortices that have putatively monosynaptic latencies of 4.5ms.
source: Similarly, electrical stimulation of the reuniens/rhomboid nucleus in rats (Di Prisco and Vertes, 2006) elicits prominent evoked potentials in prefrontal cortices that have putatively monosynaptic latencies of 4.5ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: mPFC responses to reuniens stimulation were qualitatively different from responses elicited by hippocampal stimulation, with significant differences in latency, amplitude, slope of EPSPs, and duration of hyperpolarization.
source: We found that mPFC responses to reuniens stimulation were qualitatively different from responses elicited by hippocampal stimulation, with significant differences in latency, amplitude, slope of EPSPs, and duration of hyperpolarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses to different stimulation sites.

claim: Reuniens-evoked responses occurred earlier and were more consistent than hippocampal-evoked responses, suggesting higher response fidelity in the reuniens-prefrontal pathway than in the hippocampo-cortical pathway.
source: Reuniens-evoked responses occurred earlier and were more consistent than hippocampal-evoked responses, suggesting higher response fidelity in the reuniens-prefrontal pathway than in the hippocampo-cortical pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing response properties.

claim: Both pyramidal cells and inhibitory neurons mediate the hippocampo-prefrontal response.
source: Both pyramidal cells and inhibitory neurons mediate the hippocampo-prefrontal response, with the early component thought to be primarily mediated by AMPA receptors (Dégenètais et al., 2003; Jay et al., 1992) and the early hyperpolarization was likely mediated by GABAA and the late component by either GABAB conductances (Dégenètais et al., 2003) or it was mediated by disfacilitation (Contreras et al., 1996; Fuentealba et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The early component of hippocampo-prefrontal response is thought to be primarily mediated by AMPA receptors.
source: Both pyramidal cells and inhibitory neurons mediate the hippocampo-prefrontal response, with the early component thought to be primarily mediated by AMPA receptors (Dégenètais et al., 2003; Jay et al., 1992) and the early hyperpolarization was likely mediated by GABAA and the late component by either GABAB conductances (Dégenètais et al., 2003) or it was mediated by disfacilitation (Contreras et al., 1996; Fuentealba et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The early hyperpolarization in hippocampo-prefrontal response was likely mediated by GABAA.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The late component of hyperpolarization in hippocampo-prefrontal response was mediated by either GABAB conductances or disfacilitation.

claim: mPFC interneurons respond to hippocampal stimulation with a shorter response latency than pyramidal cells.
source: mPFC interneurons also respond to hippocampal stimulation, with a shorter response latency than pyramidal cells, suggesting that the hippocampus can exert feedforward inhibition in the medial prefrontal cortex (Tierney et al., 2004), which could explain the polarity reversal of mPFC neurons response around –70 mV to hippocampal stimulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The hippocampus can exert feedforward inhibition in the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: mPFC interneurons also respond to hippocampal stimulation, with a shorter response latency than pyramidal cells, suggesting that the hippocampus can exert feedforward inhibition in the medial prefrontal cortex (Tierney et al., 2004), which could explain the polarity reversal of mPFC neurons response around –70 mV to hippocampal stimulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the shorter latency of interneuron responses and supported by citation.

claim: AMPA excitation and GABA inhibition may mediate the primary depolarizing and secondary hyperpolarizing responses to reuniens stimulation in medial prefrontal cells.
source: AMPA excitation and GABA inhibition may also mediate the primary depolarizing and secondary hyperpolarizing responses to reuniens stimulation in medial prefrontal cells (Figure 1C and F) similar to previously demonstrated mediodorsal-prefrontal pathway (Gigg et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to similar pathway.

claim: The reuniens nucleus sends glutamatergic afferents to the prefrontal cortex.
source: Similar to hippocampal afferents to the mPFC, the reuniens nucleus sends glutamatergic afferents to the prefrontal cortex (Hur and Zaborszky, 2005; Pirot et al., 1995) enabling influence on the prefrontal neuronal activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Reuniens is believed to play a critical role in connecting the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus due to its bidirectional connections with both structures.
source: Reuniens is believed to play a critical role in connecting the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus due to its bidirectional connections with both structures (Di Prisco and Vertes, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Previous research indicates the reuniens may synchronize the activity of the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: The prefrontal cortex and hippocampus are both essential for memory processing (Bontempi et al., 1999), and previous research indicates the reuniens may synchronize the activity of these two structures (Ferraris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nucleus reuniens exerts excitatory actions at the CA1.
source: Demonstrations that the nucleus reuniens exerts excitatory actions at the CA1 (Bertram and Zhang, 1999; Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997) and also at the prefrontal cortex (Di Prisco and Vertes, 2006; intracellularly confirmed and described in our study) provides supporting evidence for this claim that nucleus Reuniens might synchronize the activity of ventral hippocampus and mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nucleus reuniens exerts excitatory actions at the prefrontal cortex.
source: Demonstrations that the nucleus reuniens exerts excitatory actions at the CA1 (Bertram and Zhang, 1999; Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997) and also at the prefrontal cortex (Di Prisco and Vertes, 2006; intracellularly confirmed and described in our study) provides supporting evidence for this claim that nucleus Reuniens might synchronize the activity of ventral hippocampus and mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and experimental data from this study.

claim: The reuniens nucleus, ventral hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex form a functional loop, with the prefrontal cortex acting as a mediator of the hippocampo-prefronto-thalamic relay.
source: These results support the idea that the reuniens nucleus, ventral hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex form a functional loop, with the prefrontal cortex acting as a mediator of the hippocampo-prefronto-thalamic relay.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing overlapping response areas.

claim: The coupling of hippocampal SWRs to cortical slow waves and thalamocortical spindles is thought to be the main network mechanisms by which the brain promotes the consolidation of short-term memory into long-term storage.
source: In NREM sleep, the coupling of hippocampal SWRs to cortical slow waves and thalamocortical spindles is thought to be the main network mechanisms by which the brain promotes the consolidation of short-term memory into long-term storage (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reuniens single-unit activity was strongly modulated by ventral hippocampal SWRs.
source: We found that reuniens single-unit activity exhibited sporadic locking to ventral hippocampal theta cycles (during REM sleep) and was strongly modulated by ventral hippocampal SWRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chronic recordings.

claim: Although overall CA1 ripples suppress MD firing, at the onset of spindles, the MD firing triggered by ripples was increased.
source: These results are congruent with findings in MD thalamic nucleus showing that although overall CA1 ripples suppress MD firing, at the onset of spindles, the MD firing triggered by ripples was increased (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The firing pause in reuniens neurons during SWR and the presence of spike-bursts after SWR suggests that the spike burst is a rebound from previous hyperpolarization.
source: The firing pause in reuniens neurons during SWR and the presence of spike-bursts after SWR suggests that the spike burst is a rebound from previous hyperpolarization (Jahnsen and Llinás, 1984).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citation.

claim: SWR drive some inhibitory cells that hyperpolarize at least MD and reuniens.
source: This suggests that SWR drive some inhibitory cells that hyperpolarize at least MD and reuniens.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the firing patterns observed.

claim: If hyperpolarization is strong enough, like during slow wave, it triggers rebound spike bursts.
source: If hyperpolarization is strong enough, like during slow wave, it triggers rebound spike bursts.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of rebound mechanisms.

claim: The hippocampal modulation of reuniens activity points to a thalamic pathway for the coupling of sleep rhythms.
source: Considering the strong influence of reuniens on prefrontal targets, the hippocampal modulation of reuniens activity points to a thalamic pathway for the coupling of sleep rhythms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing hippocampal modulation of reuniens.

claim: The minimal requirement to generate spindles is the reticular thalamic nucleus (TRN).
source: Although the minimal requirement to generate spindles is the reticular thalamic nucleus (TRN; Bazhenov et al., 1999; Steriade et al., 1987), our finding of increased SWR probability and ripple power prior to the onset of thalamocortical spindles suggest that hippocampal drive through reuniens may initiate the thalamocortical cascade of events that leads to spindles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal drive through reuniens may initiate the thalamocortical cascade of events that leads to spindles.
source: Although the minimal requirement to generate spindles is the reticular thalamic nucleus (TRN; Bazhenov et al., 1999; Steriade et al., 1987), our finding of increased SWR probability and ripple power prior to the onset of thalamocortical spindles suggest that hippocampal drive through reuniens may initiate the thalamocortical cascade of events that leads to spindles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing temporal relationships.

claim: In first-order nuclei of the thalamus, cortical firing can trigger spindles by exciting hyperpolarized neurons of the TRN, eliciting high-frequency spike bursts.
source: In first-order nuclei of the thalamus, cortical firing can trigger spindles by exciting hyperpolarized neurons of the TRN, eliciting high-frequency spike bursts (Contreras and Steriade, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TRN bursts can drive IPSPs in thalamocortical neurons, eliciting rebound low-threshold calcium spikes.
source: In turn, TRN bursts can drive IPSPs in thalamocortical neurons, eliciting rebound low-threshold calcium spikes (Bazhenov et al., 1999) and developing the spindle primarily through recurrent inhibitory-excitatory interactions between the TRN and thalamocortical neurons (Contreras and Steriade, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical firing contributes to spindle synchronization and the maintenance of the spindle through its influence on the TRN.
source: Cortical firing also contributes to spindle synchronization and the maintenance of the spindle through its influence on the TRN (Bonjean et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cortical activation after the down state can initiate thalamocortical spindling and lock the timing of spindles to the phase of the slow oscillation.
source: Thus, cortical activation after the down state can initiate thalamocortical spindling and lock the timing of spindles to the phase of the slow oscillation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mechanisms described.

source: However, less is known about spindle generation in higher-order thalamic nuclei, especially in thalamic nuclei with limbic circuitry such as reuniens.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap.

claim: The reuniens is connected bidirectionally with the prefrontal cortex.
source: The circuitry is in place for spindle generation in the reuniens nucleus: The reuniens is connected bidirectionally with the prefrontal cortex (Herkenham, 1978; Vertes et al., 2007); layer 6 of the infralimbic cortex projects to the anteromedial TRN (Cornwall et al., 1990), a region that projects to the reuniens nucleus (Cavdar et al., 2008; Kolmac and Mitrofanis, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical study.

source: While reuniens nucleus neurons can generate low-threshold calcium spike, they do not display hyperpolarization-activated current (Walsh et al., 2017), likely limiting their ability to generate and maintain spindles.

claim: Without MD in the computational model, no spindles were generated.
source: Of note, without MD in our computational model, no spindles were generated (data not shown).

claim: First order thalamocortical cells display inhibitory, spindle-like activities during cortical active state.
source: In general, although first order thalamocortical cells display inhibitory, spindle-like activities during cortical active state, higher order thalamocortical cells show persistent depolarizing states, excluding their possibility to generate spindle-related rebound spike bursts (Groh et al., 2014; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal SWRs trigger thalamic rebound burst firing and precede the onset of reuniens and mPFC spindles.
source: We found that hippocampal SWRs trigger thalamic rebound burst firing and precede the onset of reuniens and mPFC spindles, which points to SWRs as one of candidate events for spindle initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chronic recordings.

claim: The strong excitatory drive emerging from the hippocampus during SWRs may represent an ontogenetically different mechanism for the initiation of spindles in the limbic circuitry.
source: In this regard, the strong excitatory drive emerging form the hippocampus during SWRs may represent an ontogenetically different mechanism for the initiation of spindles in the limbic circuitry.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: It is not yet clear whether the hippocampus influences inhibitory thalamic structures such as the TRN or the zona incerta.
source: However, the generation and maintenance of spindle cycles depend on burst firing from inhibitory structures such as the TRN. To date, it is not yet clear whether the hippocampus influences inhibitory thalamic structures such as the TRN or the zona incerta, although projections from subiculum to the rostral TRN were previously described (Cavdar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap, with citation noting some anatomical evidence.

claim: Hippocampal SWRs can initiate a cascade of thalamocortical events, beginning with the excitation of reuniens, which in turn excites the mPFC.
source: We propose that hippocampal SWRs can initiate a cascade of thalamocortical events, beginning with the excitation of reuniens, which in turn excites the mPFC. This mPFC excitation leads to spindle activity generated through cortico-thalamic feedback from the mPFC to other thalamic nuclei, such as the MD nucleus.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.
